questions.question: Influenza.

parts.text: Name two surface proteins important for pathogenesis.
What two conditions are necessary for a pandemic (antigenic shift)?

parts_raw.text: A. Name two surface proteins important for pathogenesis.
C. What two conditions are necessary for a pandemic. (antigenic shift)

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Hemagglutinin (HA) – mediates attachment to sialic acid receptors and membrane fusion. (2) Neuraminidase (NA) – cleaves sialic acid to release progeny virions and prevent aggregation.
b) Antigenic drift = relatively minor, frequent antigenic changes from gradual accumulation of point (amino-acid) mutations in the major antigenic sites of the HA (and NA). Because antibody to previous strains no longer neutralizes the variant effectively, immunologic selection lets the variant supplant prior circulating strains and cause seasonal epidemics.
c) A pandemic requires antigenic shift, i.e. (1) emergence of a novel influenza A virus with a radically different HA (and/or NA) subtype toward which the population has little or no prior immunity, and (2) the virus being capable of efficient, sustained person-to-person transmission.

cohort_answer.text:
Hemaglutinin; Neuramidase
Minor antigenic changes in NA/HA due to mutations introduced during replication, with selection during an epidemic due to reduced immunogenicity of these variants
Emergence of antigenically variant influenza virus toward which the population has little to no prior immunity, leading to global spread of human influenza caused by a new influenza subtype; Easily transmissible

questions.question: Patient with H5N1 influenza. List four infection-control interventions.

parts.text: What are four infection control interventions?

parts_raw.text: What are 4 interventions from infection control?

questions.model_answer: (1) Place the patient on droplet plus contact precautions, ideally in a single/negative-pressure room with cohorting of confirmed cases. (2) Add airborne precautions (N95 respirators, negative-pressure isolation) during aerosol-generating procedures. (3) Hand hygiene and appropriate personal protective equipment (gown, gloves, eye protection) for all staff. (4) Antiviral treatment of the case and oseltamivir post-exposure prophylaxis plus monitoring of exposed contacts/health care workers.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell's transmission section supports masks, negative-pressure isolation and N95 use for aerosols; the discrete IPAC bundle (cohorting, precautions tiers, PPE, prophylaxis) reflects WHO/CDC/PHAC avian influenza infection-control guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Cohorting of patient; Rapid diagnostics; Treatment; Droplet precautions; Airborne precautions for AGMPs; Prophylaxis.

questions.question: A patient has H5N1 avian influenza.
questions.model_answer:
(1) Place the patient immediately in a single room — ideally a negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room — with the door closed and dedicated equipment; restrict visitors and limit patient movement outside the room.
(2) Apply contact + droplet precautions with eye protection, escalated to airborne precautions (N95/fit-tested respirator) for all care and especially for aerosol-generating procedures.
(3) Strict hand hygiene before and after contact and after PPE removal, with trained donning/doffing and readily available PPE.
(4) Active surveillance and triage/screening at entry (travel and poultry exposure screen), rapid notification of the laboratory and public health, monitoring of exposed healthcare workers for 7-10 days, with oseltamivir post-exposure prophylaxis and seasonal influenza vaccination for staff.
questions.beyond_mandell: WHO/PHAC avian influenza infection prevention guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Enhanced droplet/contact precautions for avian flu. Organizational controls: facility design (single rooms, accessibility to PPEs), policies and procedures, triage/screening/assessment. Patients with compatible symptoms and/or travel should be promptly placed in droplet contact precautions. Surveillance, laboratory testing/reporting. Respiratory hygiene, hand hygiene. Patient flow/activities restricted, management of visitors. Appropriate PPE - contact/droplet precautions. Education of healthcare personnel

questions.question: Live-attenuated influenza vaccine.

parts.text: What is the reason it is recommended by NACI for ages 2 to 17 years?
What is the route of administration?
Why is it not recommended for age less than 24 months?
Name four contraindications other than anaphylaxis to vaccine components.

parts_raw.text: What is the reason it is recommended by NACI for ages 2-17?
What is the route of administration?
Why is it not recommended for age < 24 months?
Name 4 contraindications other than anaphylaxis to vaccine components?

questions.model_answer:
a) LAIV replicates in the nasopharyngeal mucosa and induces local secretory IgA plus cell-mediated and cross-reactive immunity, which in early trials gave superior efficacy to inactivated vaccine in young children; it also requires no needle, improving acceptability and uptake. NACI no longer states a preferential recommendation over inactivated vaccine — either LAIV or IIV may be used in children 2–17 years, and LAIV remains a reasonable option in this age group.

b) Intranasal spray (0.1 mL into each nostril).

c) No. Egg allergy of any severity is not a contraindication to influenza vaccine, including LAIV; residual ovalbumin content is negligible and vaccine may be given in any setting without special precautions or prior skin testing.

d) Because of a small but statistically significant excess of medically attended wheezing and hospitalization in the 2–4 weeks after vaccination in children under 24 months.

e) (1) Immunocompromising conditions or immunosuppressive therapy (including household setting requiring a protective environment). (2) Severe asthma — current active wheezing, or on high-dose/oral corticosteroids, or medically attended wheezing within the previous 7 days. (3) Children and adolescents 2–17 years on chronic acetylsalicylic acid therapy (Reye syndrome risk). (4) Pregnancy. Also: history of Guillain-Barré syndrome within 6 weeks of a previous influenza vaccine. Precautions: significant nasal congestion; avoid influenza antivirals from 48 hours before to 2 weeks after; avoid close contact with severely immunocompromised persons for 2 weeks.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI seasonal influenza statement: LAIV no longer preferentially recommended over IIV in children 2–17; egg allergy is not a contraindication to any influenza vaccine.

cohort_answer.text: A) [Note: outdated - LAIV no longer preferentially recommended over IIV in children 2-17 per NACI review]. B) Intranasal. C) No - only trace amounts of ovalbumin, very low chance of reaction. D) Small but significant increased rate of wheezing 2-4 weeks following vaccination in this age group. E) Immunocompromised; severe asthma (current active wheezing, oral/high-dose inhaled steroids, or medically attended wheezing in past 7 days); children 2-17 on chronic ASA therapy (Reye's syndrome risk); pregnancy (lack of safety data); GBS onset within 6 weeks of prior influenza vaccination without other known cause. Cautions: avoid if significant nasal congestion; avoid close contact with immunocompromised individuals for 2 weeks after vaccine; wait 48h after antivirals before vaccine or 2 weeks after vaccine before antivirals.

questions.question: Influenza pathogenesis.

parts.text: How does viral infection predispose to bacterial infection?

parts_raw.text: A. How viral infection predispose to bacterial infection

questions.model_answer: a) Influenza virus infects and kills respiratory columnar epithelial cells (necrosis and apoptosis) causing desquamation and loss of the ciliated epithelium, which impairs the mucociliary clearance apparatus that normally removes bacteria. Destruction of the epithelial barrier exposes basement membrane and receptors that promote bacterial adherence and colonization, and virus-altered colonization can change replication/toxin production of organisms such as staphylococci. The result is secondary bacterial pneumonia, most commonly with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus.
questions.beyond_mandell: The finer immune mechanisms in the cohort answer (downregulated antimicrobial peptides; impaired alveolar macrophage/neutrophil/NK function) are established influenza immunology beyond what this chapter states explicitly.

cohort_answer.text:
Numerous alterations of the respiratory epithelium and host immune responses occur during influenza virus infection that predisposes a host to coinfection with bacterial pathogens:
As influenza virus infects and kills host cells, epithelial surfaces become exposed and permissive to bacterial attachment.
Physical barriers (e.g., mucociliary transport) are damaged, pathogen detection is decreased
Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are downregulated, receptors are upregulated, virus production is enhanced, bacterial transepithelial migration is permitted, and repair mechanisms are lost.
Several host responses are also dampened, altered, or removed.
Alveolar macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells, and NK cells have altered cytokine profiles and become impaired and/or depleted. These changes result in a heightened inflammatory environment with decreased bacterial surveillance and eradication

Influenza causes desquamation or loss of ciliated columnar epithelium
Decreased pathogen detection
Reduced clearance of bacteria from epithelial surfaces

questions.question: Use of antiviral agents against influenza, including indications and a comparison of amantadine, oseltamivir, and zanamivir.
questions.question_raw:
Q3 (2009 AM)
Indication for antivirals against influenza
Adult Risk Factors:

parts.text: State the adult risk factors / indications for antiviral treatment of influenza.

Compare and contrast amantadine, oseltamivir, and zanamivir with respect to mechanism, the stage of the viral life cycle affected, side effects, and whether they are sensitive or resistant to seasonal (non-pandemic) H1N1, swine-origin H1N1, H5N1, and H3N2.

parts_raw.text: Adult Risk Factors: (what are the indications/risk factors for antiviral treatment in adults)

Compare and contrast amantadine, oseltamivir, zanamivir with respect so mechanism, viral life cycle affected, side effect, whether sensitive or resistant to seasonal H1N1 non pandemic, H1N1 swine, H5N1 and H3N2

questions.model_answer:
a) High-risk adults (treat as early as possible): (1) age ≥65 yr; (2) chronic pulmonary, cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, hematologic, metabolic (e.g. diabetes) or neurologic disease; (3) immunocompromise, morbid obesity, pregnancy/≤2 wk postpartum, long-term-care residents, and all hospitalized patients.
b) High-risk children: (1) age <5 yr (especially <2 yr); (2) chronic medical conditions, immunocompromise, or neurologic/neurodevelopmental disorders; (3) long-term aspirin therapy (Reye syndrome risk).
c) Amantadine — M2 ion-channel inhibitor; blocks early viral uncoating (and late HA maturation); CNS/GI side effects (nervousness, confusion, insomnia); RESISTANT to seasonal H1N1 (since 2008-09), A(H1N1)pdm09 "swine", H5N1, and H3N2 (>95% resistant) — essentially no useful activity against current strains. Oseltamivir — oral neuraminidase inhibitor; blocks virion release/spread (late); nausea/vomiting; SENSITIVE to swine A(H1N1)pdm09, H5N1, and H3N2, but seasonal H1N1 was widely RESISTANT (H275Y, 2007-08). Zanamivir — inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor; blocks virion release/spread (late); bronchospasm/respiratory side effects; SENSITIVE to seasonal H1N1, swine A(H1N1)pdm09, H5N1, and H3N2 (retains activity against oseltamivir H275Y-resistant strains).
questions.beyond_mandell: The treatment indications / adult and pediatric risk-factor lists are from IDSA seasonal influenza guidance, not this Mandell chapter; the chapter supports only the mechanism, life-cycle, toxicity, and sensitivity/resistance comparison.

cohort_answer.text:
A - IDSA indications for treatment: Clinicians should start antiviral treatment as soon as possible for adults and children with documented or suspected influenza, irrespective of influenza vaccination history, who meet the following criteria: Persons of any age who are hospitalized with influenza, regardless of illness duration prior to hospitalization (A-II). Outpatients of any age with severe or progressive illness, regardless of illness duration (A-III). Outpatients who are at high risk of complications from influenza, including those with chronic medical conditions and immunocompromised patients (A-II). Children younger than 2 years and adults >=65 years (A-III). Pregnant women and those within 2 weeks postpartum (A-III). Clinicians can consider antiviral treatment for adults and children who are not at high risk of influenza complications, with documented or suspected influenza, irrespective of influenza vaccination history, who are either: Outpatients with illness onset <=2 days before presentation (C-I). Symptomatic outpatients who are household contacts of persons who are at high risk of developing complications from influenza, particularly those who are severely immunocompromised (C-III). Symptomatic healthcare providers who care for patients who are at high risk of developing complications from influenza, particularly those who are severely immunocompromised (C-III)

Adult Risk Factors list: Age >65, Chronic lung disease, CV/Renal/Liver disease, Hematologic, Metabolic condition, Immunosuppression, Neurological deficit/dementia, Obesity, LTC resident, Indigenous, pregnant

Pediatric Risk Factors (Last year's answer): Age <4 (especially if <2), Chronic medical conditions, Immunosuppression, Cognitive dysfunction/seizure/NM disorder, Long term ASA use (risk of Reye syndrome), Resident of CCC

Drug comparison table (partial, sensitivity columns for amantadine/rimantadine/oseltamivir/zanamivir order unclear): Activity against H1N1 non-pandemic | Sensitive | sensitive | Resistant | Resistant. Activity against H1N1 swine | Sensitive | Sensitive | Sensitive | sensitive. Activity against H5N1 | | | | Susceptible. Activity against H3N2 | Resistant | Resistant | | Susceptible

questions.question: Influenza.

parts.text: Describe/explain the issues around influenza pandemic potential and avian influenza.

parts_raw.text: A. Describe/explain issues around influenza pandemic potential and avian influenza

questions.model_answer: a) Birds are the major reservoir of influenza A diversity, harbouring all 16 HA and all 9 NA subtypes, usually with mild or asymptomatic (fecal) shedding. Pandemics arise when a novel avian-origin HA (± NA) enters humans with no prior population immunity. Direct avian-to-human transmission (e.g. H5N1, H7N9, H9N2) is usually limited: avian HA prefers α2-3 sialic-acid–galactose receptors whereas human airway favours α2-6, restricting replication and human-to-human spread, and non-HA genes further limit host range. Two routes overcome this barrier: (1) genetic reassortment when an intermediate host such as the pig (which carries both α2-3 and α2-6 receptors, a "mixing vessel") is co-infected with avian and human viruses, combining novel surface glycoproteins with human-adapted internal genes (as in 1957, 1968, and the 2009 pH1N1 quadruple reassortant); and (2) gradual adaptation of an avian/swine virus to humans (as proposed for 1918). Only a few mutations (in the polymerase, HA receptor binding and HA acid stability) may be needed for an H5 virus to gain airborne transmissibility, so ongoing surveillance of avian strains for these markers is critical.

cohort_answer.text:
Birds have all 16 HA subtypes and all 9 NA subtypes in their circulating influenza A viruses. Past pandemics resulted from novel reassortments of virus that passed from birds to humans, sometimes with other mammals as intermediaries. H9, H7, H5 variants have all been tracked to birds. Most transmission events seem to result in mild disease, small number of people affected and limited human to human transmission. More recent cases have been tracked directly to live bird markets (e.g. of H7N9) and felt to have limited inter-human transmissibility.
Avian strains prefer receptors with different sialic acid-galactose linkages than what is present in humans, therefore rare to have coinfection in humans -> Need third species, like a pig, with receptors for both strains where reassortment can occur. Also non-HA genes may mediate this restriction of hosts and replication further.
Avian strains can also adapt to human hosts through evolution in swine with multiple receptors, even without the presence of human virus (e.g. a drift mechanism).

questions.question: Three cases of influenza occur on a hospital hematology/oncology ward, two confirmed as influenza A.
questions.question_raw:
Q6 (2003 AM)
3 cases of influenza, 2 of which are confirmed as influenza A in a hospital heme/onc ward.

parts.text: State the advantages and disadvantages of each.

parts_raw.text: What are three methods of prophylaxis?
B. What are the advantages and disadvantages of each?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Antiviral chemoprophylaxis of patients (neuraminidase inhibitor, e.g. oseltamivir once daily). (2) Antiviral chemoprophylaxis of exposed health-care workers/staff. (3) Vaccination (immunoprophylaxis) of patients and staff; plus standard outbreak infection-control measures.
b) Chemoprophylaxis of patients — advantages: immediate protective effect, prevents spread to high-risk hosts, effective for controlling/preventing nosocomial outbreaks and additive to vaccine; disadvantages: cost, drug side effects, not all eligible (GI/renal), must recognize the outbreak first, and can select antiviral resistance. Chemoprophylaxis of HCWs — advantages: immediate effect, limits staff-to-patient transmission and sick days; disadvantages: cost, side effects, adherence, risk of selecting resistance. Vaccination (immunoprophylaxis) — advantages: durable, can be given pre-season, no ongoing drug administration, fewer GI side effects, protection additive to antivirals; disadvantages: ~2-week delay to protection (inadequate for an active outbreak), reduced efficacy in immunocompromised hosts or with poor strain match, and contraindications in some patients.
questions.beyond_mandell: The structured advantages/disadvantages and the defined prophylaxis durations derive from IDSA/PHAC outbreak-control guidance; the chapter grounds only that chemoprophylaxis is effective for nosocomial influenza, is additive to vaccine, can select resistance, and that vaccine protection is delayed.

cohort_answer.text:
Part 1: Antiviral chemoprophylaxis - Preexposure: > 3mo and high risk group, give for the whole season. Post exposure e.g. PrEP and PEP, either to patients or to healthcare workers. In setting of outbreak on ward generally give for at least 2 weeks and one week after onset of last illness. If exposed and able to be vaccinated, vaccine can be given followed by PEP for 2 weeks if good match. Immunoprophylaxis - generally given as PrEP. (NOTES: PEP: Within 48 hrs and for 7 days only in outbreak settings and special situations.)

Part B: Chemoprophylaxis to patients - Advantages: Immediate effect, prevent spread to high risk patients. Disadvantages: Cost, patient side effects, not all patients eligible e.g. GI tract issues, Need to recognize outbreak before implementation. Can promote resistance.
Chemoprophylaxis to HCW - Advantages: Immediate effect, prevent spread to high risk patients as often mediated by healthcare workers moving from room to room; can limit sick days and presenteeism. Disadvantages: Cost, side effects, need to recognize outbreak before implementation, can promote resistance.
Immunoprophylaxis of patients and healthcare workers: Advantages: Can be implemented in advance to prevent outbreak; can cover non-outbreak strains; does not require on-going drug administration and less GI side effects. Disadvantages: Delayed effect of 2 weeks for full benefit, during which may contract illness, certain patients may have contraindications to vaccine, May be ineffective if weak immune system or poor match, Cost (cost effective for high risk patients but perhaps not for healthy adults), side effects

questions.question: For each of the following viruses, state whether it is a DNA or RNA virus, whether it is enveloped or non-enveloped, and name an antiviral used for treatment (not immunotherapy): measles, mumps, Epstein-Barr virus, Zika, Ebola, influenza, hepatitis B, coronavirus.
questions.question_raw: AM 16. List of viruses - name whether it is DNA/RNA, Enveloped/not, and name an antiviral used for treatment (not immunotherapy) (whole chart - 3): Measles, Mumps, EBV, Zika, Ebola, Influenza, Hepatitis B (and Coronavirus)
questions.model_answer: a) Measles: ssRNA, negative-sense (Paramyxoviridae); enveloped; no specific antiviral (vitamin A supportive; ribavirin only anecdotal in severe/immunocompromised disease). Mumps: ssRNA, negative-sense (Paramyxoviridae); enveloped; no specific antiviral - supportive care. Epstein-Barr virus: dsDNA (Herpesviridae); enveloped; no proven antiviral (herpesvirus DNA-polymerase inhibitors such as acyclovir/ganciclovir reduce shedding but not disease). Zika: ssRNA, positive-sense (Flaviviridae); enveloped; no specific antiviral - supportive care. Ebola: ssRNA, negative-sense (Filoviridae); enveloped; no small-molecule antiviral of proven benefit (remdesivir studied; licensed agents are monoclonal antibodies, i.e., immunotherapy). Influenza: segmented ssRNA, negative-sense (Orthomyxoviridae); enveloped; neuraminidase inhibitors - oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir (or baloxavir). Hepatitis B: partially double-stranded circular DNA (Hepadnaviridae); enveloped; nucleos(t)ide polymerase inhibitors - entecavir, tenofovir (or interferon-alfa). Coronavirus: ssRNA, positive-sense; enveloped with club-shaped spikes; remdesivir/nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for SARS-CoV-2.
questions.beyond_mandell: Baloxavir and SARS-CoV-2-specific agents (remdesivir, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir) postdate/lie outside this chapter; per IDSA influenza 2018 and IDSA COVID-19 guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Measles - Paramyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: nothing (ribavirin trialed in severe cases, vitamin A). Mumps - Paramyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: nothing. EBV - Herpesviridae, dsDNA, enveloped: nothing (GCV, cidofovir tried). Zika - Flaviviridae, ssRNA(+), enveloped: nothing. Ebola - Filovirus, ssRNA(-), enveloped: remdesivir, or Ervebo vaccine. Influenza - Orthomyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: Oseltamivir/zanamivir/baloxavir. Hepatitis B - Hepadnaviridae, partially ds/partly ss circular DNA, enveloped: tenofovir, lamivudine, entecavir. Chikungunya - Togaviridae, ssRNA(+), enveloped: no Rx. Coronavirus - positive sense ssRNA, enveloped with club-shaped spikes.
